item: DiMasi 2016 full text: per-phase cost table read from the original article
queries_tried: WebSearch 'DiMasi Grabowski Hansen 2016 Journal of Health Economics innovation in the pharmaceutical industry R&D cost 2558 million'; WebFetch kinampark.com PDF mirror (twice); WebFetch sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167629616000291; WebFetch pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26928437; WebFetch csdd.tufts.edu/cost-study; WebFetch scholars.duke.edu/display/pub1123333
failure_reason: The publisher page returns HTTP 403 and the only open PDF mirror returned HTTP 503 on both attempts. PubMed returned a cookie-consent stub. The Tufts CSDD page carries the citation but no methods detail.
alt_sources_tried: 1) ScienceDirect publisher page (403). 2) PubMed abstract (cookie wall). 3) kinampark.com PDF mirror (503 x2). 4) Tufts CSDD cost-study page (citation only). 5) Duke Scholars record (abstract text recovered). 6) Knowledge Portalia compilation (per-phase table recovered).
best_estimate: Headline figures are firm: out-of-pocket 1395 USD million and capitalized 2558 USD million (2013 dollars), 106 compounds from 10 firms, 10.5 percent real discount rate, 2870 USD million including post-approval R&D, 8.5 percent real annual growth. Per-stage split: preclinical 430 out-of-pocket / 1098 capitalized; clinical 965 / 1460.
best_estimate_basis: Headline figures verified from the Duke Scholars abstract record (E-1001, E-1002, E-1003), which reproduces the published abstract. The per-stage split (E-1004) comes from a compilation page and is independently corroborated by Wouters 2020, which states in its own text that DiMasi assumes a 42.9 percent preclinical share; 1098/2558 = 42.9 percent, so the two agree to the decimal. Confidence in the split is therefore materially higher than a single secondary citation would warrant, but the article text itself was not read.

item: Ringel et al. 2020 'Breaking Eroom's Law' numeric series (NMEs per billion USD R&D by period)
queries_tried: WebSearch 'Ringel Scannell Baedeker Schulze 2020 Nature Reviews Drug Discovery Breaking Eroom's Law R&D efficiency NME per billion'; WebFetch media.nature.com magazine-assets PDF
failure_reason: The PDF fetched successfully but its three panels are raster figures with no underlying data table, and the small-model summary of the file produced period figures that could not be tied to any caption or axis label in the extracted text. Asserting those numbers would be inventing data.
alt_sources_tried: 1) media.nature.com PDF (figures are images). 2) nature.com article page (auth redirect). 3) PubMed record 32300238 (title and citation only). 4) ResearchGate record (request-full-text wall).
best_estimate: The paper's thesis and its three metrics are recorded without numbers (E-1044). For the approvals-versus-spend question the series is instead built directly from two primary series: FDA approval counts 2000-2024 (E-1038, E-1039) and PhRMA member R&D 1984-2022 (E-1041), combined in E-1098.
best_estimate_basis: Building the ratio from the two underlying primary series is stronger than quoting a secondary chart, because the denominator caveats can be stated explicitly. E-1098 records that the ratio uses nominal dollars, mismatched sponsor populations and no lag, and therefore is not a productivity estimate.

item: Light and Warburton 2011 full text and the derivation of their median cost figure
queries_tried: WebSearch 'Light Warburton 2011 Demythologizing the high costs of pharmaceutical research BioSocieties criticism DiMasi tax subsidies selection bias median cost'; WebFetch link.springer.com/article/10.1057/biosoc.2010.40; WebFetch health-rights.org record page
failure_reason: Springer issues a 303 redirect into an identity-provider authorisation URL. The open repository record carries a one-paragraph description without the abstract or the cost derivation.
alt_sources_tried: 1) Springer article page (auth redirect). 2) health-rights.org record (description only). 3) ResearchGate record (request-full-text wall). 4) Semantic Scholar record (metadata only).
best_estimate: Their central methodological objection is verified: the Tufts estimate is built on a high-cost subsample and then generalised, which they argue inflates the average roughly sevenfold; the reported median figure is 59.4 USD million.
best_estimate_basis: Recorded as E-1010 with circular_risk set true and a derivation note stating that provenance is only two hops. The 59.4 million figure is carried in the CSV strictly as the low bound of the published range and is never averaged with the other estimates. The qualitative objection is separately corroborated by Wouters 2020, which independently shows the observed preclinical share (12.4 percent median) is far below DiMasi's assumed 42.9 percent, an assumption-driven inflation of the same kind.

best_estimate: A CDER-plus-CBER combined annual series 2000-2024 is recorded in full (E-1039). Subtracting the CDER-only series (E-1038) year by year gives an implied CBER contribution of 17 in 2000, 12 in 2024, 17 in 2023 and 8 in 2022. For cell and gene therapy specifically: 8 novel approvals in 2024, 7 in 2023, roughly 35 cumulative (E-1053).
best_estimate_basis: The subtraction is arithmetic on two series from the same FDA-derived dataset, so it is internally consistent, but it is flagged here rather than written into the evidence ledger as a fact because the two series may use slightly different inclusion rules for CDER-reviewed biologics. The cell and gene therapy counts come from trade analysis of FDA actions and are the best available until the CBER pages become fetchable.

item: Korea MFDS annual new drug approval counts
queries_tried: WebSearch 'Korea MFDS new drug approvals per year Japan PMDA number of new active substances approved 2023 2024 review time months'; WebFetch mfds.go.kr/eng/brd/m_19/view.do?seq=70440 (2024 Drug Approval Report landing page)
failure_reason: The MFDS English landing page carries only a download link; the report itself is a Korean-language PDF attachment that the fetch tool did not retrieve.

best_estimate: The verified Korea datapoint is the review-timeline reform: target total approval time cut from about 420 days to about 295 days effective 1 January 2025 (E-1051). An observed annual count of MFDS novel approvals is not established.
best_estimate_basis: For the JP-KR region the quantitative anchor in this dataset is therefore PMDA, where CIRS gives 53 new active substances and a 290-day median approval time for 2024 (E-1032, E-1050). Korea is represented by the regulatory-timeline datapoint only, and the CSV says so in the row rather than carrying an invented approval count.

failure_reason: The Wiley article returned HTTP 403 and the Nature commentary issues a 303 authorisation redirect. CIRS covers six agencies and does not include NMPA, so no like-for-like median exists in the comparative dataset.
alt_sources_tried: 1) Wiley Clinical Pharmacology and Therapeutics article (403). 2) Nature Reviews Drug Discovery NMPA 2024 commentary (auth redirect). 3) CIRS R&D Briefing 101 (NMPA not covered). 4) NMPA English site announcements on clinical trial review optimisation (recovered, but cover IND not NDA timelines).
best_estimate: China is represented by an approval-volume datapoint (228 NDAs approved in 2024: 123 chemical, 93 biological, 12 traditional Chinese medicine, E-1049) and by the published standard NDA review target of roughly 12 to 18 months from acceptance. The CSV records the 15-month midpoint explicitly labelled as a target rather than an observed median.
best_estimate_basis: Labelling it a target keeps it from being read as comparable to the FDA 356-day and EMA 430-day observed medians. The NMPA 2024 NDA count also uses a broader denominator than FDA novel drug approvals, which the CSV row states.

The stage-resolved cost models (DiMasi, Paul, Sertkaya) pool modalities or split only small molecule versus large molecule. The ASCO educational review returned 403 and the Molecular Therapy article returned 403.
alt_sources_tried: 1) DiMasi 2016 via compilation (small versus large molecule split only, recovered). 2) Sertkaya 2024 (therapeutic area split, no modality split). 3) Sabatini and Chalmers 2023 (cell and gene aggregate only). 4) ASCO Educational Book CAR-T economics review (403). 5) Molecular Therapy gene therapy development review (403). 6) Insights Bio CAR-T cost analysis (recovered). 7) American Pharmaceutical Review AAV cost modelling (recovered).
best_estimate: What is established by modality: probability of success at the modality level for ten modalities from the BIO 2011-2020 report (E-1024); Phase I to III cost split by large versus small molecule from DiMasi (E-1004); whole-programme cost for cell and gene therapy (E-1045); and unit manufacturing economics for CAR-T (95,780 USD per dose cost of goods, 3 to 5 week vein-to-vein) and AAV (about 2 USD million per 200-litre cGMP batch).

item: Between-phase white space from Phase I to Phase II
queries_tried: WebSearch 'white space between clinical trial phases drug development cycle time gap Phase I to Phase II start months Tufts CSDD analysis'; WebFetch appliedclinicaltrialsonline.com white space article; WebFetch clinicaltrialsarena.com white space article
failure_reason: The Applied Clinical Trials page returned HTTP 403. The recoverable Tufts CSDD result states directly that the Phase I to Phase II transition time could not be reliably measured because of wide variation in the early-stage activity supporting development programmes.
alt_sources_tried: 1) Applied Clinical Trials article (403; content recovered via search result text). 2) Clinical Trials Arena sponsored article (recovered). 3) Tufts CSDD whitepapers index (no matching open document). 4) BIO 2011-2020 report inter-phase intervals (recovered, and these already contain white space).
best_estimate: The Phase II to Phase III white space is 17 months on average for the 82 percent of non-expedited programmes that have any (E-1036). For Phase I to Phase II, the best available bound is the difference between the BIO mean inter-phase interval of 2.3 years and the Wong/Siah/Lo median Phase 1 trial duration of 1.6 years, which implies roughly 8 months of non-trial time.
best_estimate_basis: That 8-month implied gap mixes two different sources and two different central tendencies (mean interval versus median duration), so it is stated here as a bound rather than entered in the evidence ledger as a measurement. The measured Phase II to Phase III value of 17 months is the one carried into the CSV.

item: Sertkaya 2024 Phase 4 mean cost as a single figure
queries_tried: WebSearch 'Sertkaya 2024 JAMA Network Open Costs of Drug Development and Research and Development Intensity in the US, 2000-2018'; WebFetch pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11214120; WebFetch aspe.hhs.gov drug-development.pdf; WebFetch aspe.hhs.gov clinical trial costs report page
failure_reason: The PMC full text yielded every other Table 1 value but the Phase 4 cost cell did not come through the extraction. Both ASPE-hosted source documents returned HTTP 403.
alt_sources_tried: 1) PMC full text (all other Table 1 values recovered). 2) ASPE drug-development.pdf (403). 3) ASPE examination-of-clinical-trial-costs report page (403). 4) JAMA Network article page (not fetched; publisher wall). 5) Sertkaya 2016 Clinical Trials paper via search (per-study Phase 2 and Phase 3 ranges recovered).
best_estimate: The Phase 4 duration is established at 36.6 months (E-1014). For Phase 4 cost the best anchor is PhRMA's 2022 functional split, where Phase IV absorbs 11,597.6 USD million, or 11.5 percent of member R&D, which exceeds both Phase I (8.5 percent) and Phase II (11.1 percent).
best_estimate_basis: The PhRMA figure is a different construct (one year of industry-wide outlay rather than per-approval cost) and the CSV labels it as such. It is nonetheless the more decision-relevant number for the S9 stage, because it measures how much cash the post-approval stage actually consumes rather than how much a model allocates to it.
